To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) risk models such as credit ratings are subject to a high degree of systematic risk; (ii) the systematic risk in ratings can be captured by a model that includes systematic risk and parameter estimation uncertainty; (iii) the model is able to produce a range for risk measures consistent, ex post, with realized losses; and (iv) this is consistent with financial markets being taken by surprise in terms of realized losses.
the global financial crisis exposed risk models such as credit ratings and value-at-risk (VaR) to large degrees of systematic risk and uncertainty.

the financial crisis exposed financial markets to severe losses in relation to securitized mortgages and that risk models such a ratings are exposed to systematic risk and parameter risk, which explains how financial markets where taken by surprise in this respect.

the financial crisis was caused by the combination of the following factors: (i) a large degree of risk model systematic risk and parameter risk, and (ii) an unexpected large increase in the correlation between the default risk of mortgage-backed securities and the market risk of financial institutions.

financial institutions should not rely on risk models that are not designed to deal with parameter uncertainty.
